VIDEO.title: THIS Is What Really Destroys Marriage
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 19:1-12. Jesus leaves Galilee for the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Pharisees test Him: is it lawful to divorce a wife for any reason at all? He answers from creation, male and female, one flesh: what God has joined together, let no man separate. Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart; whoever divorces except for sexual immorality and marries another commits adultery. The disciples conclude it is better not to marry, and Jesus speaks of eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom.

Jesus is heading to Jerusalem, and the Pharisees are already plotting (12:14). The question may be a trap: Herod Antipas had married his brother's wife Herodias and killed John the Baptist for speaking against it, not far from where Jesus stands.

The question is really about the first-century debate over 'some indecency' in Deuteronomy 24:1. The school of Shammai allowed divorce only for unchastity; the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any reason. Jesus agrees with the stricter reading, but grounds marriage in Genesis 1 and 2, before Sinai.

Neither Deuteronomy 24 nor Exodus 21:10-11 commands divorce; they regulate a situation already happening and protect the wife. 'Hardness of heart' echoes Psalm 95, where Israel did not know God's ways.

The lesson: those who truly seek to know God will properly interpret His commandments. Proper motivation guides proper interpretation. The Pharisees read Torah to know Torah; read it to know God (Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 9:23-24).
QUOTES: Instead of reading Torah to know God, they got caught up in reading Torah to know Torah.
This one-fleshness has the power to withstand badly cooked meals.
Marriage is an agreement between three persons: the husband, the wife, and the Lord.

method.p: Jesus answers a question about Moses by going back before Moses, to creation. The teacher calls it reading from the earliest word: what God did 'from the beginning' (19:4, 8) sets the frame for what Moses later permitted.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Have you not read that He who created them from the beginning made them male and female,
So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.

but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am Yahweh who shows lovingkindness, justice, and righteousness on earth; for I delight in these things,” declares Yahweh.

left.text: And some Pharisees came to Jesus, testing Him and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason at all?”

right.text: For when Herod had John arrested, he bound him and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip.

lines.text: Matthew does not say they wanted a charge, as in John 8:6, but we know they were conspiring to destroy Him (12:14). The question is probably not innocent.
Perhaps they hoped to embroil Jesus in Herod's drama. John was imprisoned and beheaded not far from where Jesus now stands.

src.text: “If a man takes a wife and marries her, and it happens that she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out from his house,

lines.text: In the Hebrew the phrase can be read 'a thing of nakedness,' sexual immorality, or 'a naked thing,' anything out of order in the marriage. Two first-century schools took the two sides.
The Mishnah records it: 'Beit Shammai say: A man may not divorce his wife unless he finds out about her having engaged in a matter of forbidden sexual intercourse' (Mishnah Gittin 9:10).
Hillel put weight on 'she finds no favor in his eyes' and let the husband define what was out of order, so divorce could follow for the silliest of reasons, like a bad meal.

The Mishnah: 'Beit Hillel say: He may divorce her even due to a minor issue, e.g., because she burned or over-salted his dish' (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). It credits the 'better looking' reason to Rabbi Akiva: 'even if he found another woman who is better looking than her' (Mishnah Gittin 9:10).

left.text: then her former husband who sent her away is not allowed to take her again to be his wife, since she has been defiled; for that is an abomination before Yahweh, and you shall not bring sin on the land which Yahweh your God gives you as an inheritance.

right.text: And if he will not do these three things for her, then she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.

lines.text: These are the two main passages rabbis looked to on divorce. Neither commands men to divorce their wives. They acknowledge it is already happening and deal with a related issue: the wife's protection.
So when the Pharisees ask why Moses 'commanded' a certificate (19:7), Jesus answers that he 'permitted' it (19:8). Moses gave no command to divorce.

left.text: And God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.

right.text: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and cleave to his wife; and they shall become one flesh.

lines.text: Jesus does not say 'I side with Shammai.' He grounds marriage in the creation account, which comes before whatever Moses decided at Sinai: one marriage, one flesh, for life.
This one-fleshness images God. It has the power to withstand badly cooked meals, arguments, strife, and any old reason people come up with.

src.text: So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.”

lines.text: Marriage is greater than an agreement between two people: husband, wife and the Lord. To divorce inappropriately is to violate an agreement with God.
It is not the pastor who joins people in marriage; whoever officiates merely affirms what God is doing. Jesus also puts the onus on husbands, not wives (19:8-9).

left.text: He *said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it has not been this way.

right.text: For forty years I loathed that generation, / And said they are a people who wander in their heart, / And they do not know My ways.

lines.text: The phrase is probably an allusion to Psalm 95:8-11: 'Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah' (Psalms 95:8), when Israel tested God in the wilderness and did not know His ways.
Isn't that what the Pharisees are doing now, testing Jesus? The commands at Sinai were meant to reform the practice of divorce over time.

left.text: And I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.”

right.text: but I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except for the reason of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

lines.text: The only permission Jesus allows is porneia, sexual immorality, recalling the Sermon on the Mount. It is a broad term, but it narrowed things considerably for first-century Jews.

src.text: For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are also eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to accept this, let him accept it.”

lines.text: The disciples struggle with the stricter view. Jesus says in so many words: if you have a problem with the sacredness and finality of marriage, don't get married. Be a eunuch for the sake of God's kingdom.
In the first century there were two kinds of eunuchs: those born without reproductive parts, and those castrated to serve as royal or government officials.

KNOWGOD.title: If you had known what this means

left.text: But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent.

right.text: For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, / And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

lines.text: How could teachers who memorized God's law miss the point of divorce? Jesus already told us when His disciples were challenged over the Sabbath: they would not have condemned them if they understood the heart of God.

KNOWGOD.title: That he understands and knows Me

src.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Let not a wise man boast in his wisdom, and let not the mighty man boast in his might; let not a rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am Yahweh who shows lovingkindness, justice, and righteousness on earth; for I delight in these things,” declares Yahweh.

lines.text: It has always been God's desire that His people know Him. Someone who camps out in Genesis 1 and 2 to know the God who reveals Himself there would not be surprised by Jesus' answer.
The Pharisees were entrusted with the oracles of God (Romans 3:2), yet read Torah to know Torah instead of to know God: the same activity with two different motivations.
Those who truly seek to know God will properly interpret His commandments, because they understand the heart behind them. Those who seek only to know His commandments will often misinterpret them.

The teacher describes studying theology early on to know what God's word said, and later learning from a mentor to read it to know God. The result is greater intimacy with the Lord and a deeper love for Him.

BACKGROUND.p: A husband could divorce by giving a certificate; a wife generally could not initiate. The Mishnah records three views on Deuteronomy 24:1: Shammai's (only sexual misconduct), Hillel's (even a burned dish) and Rabbi Akiva's (even finding someone better looking) (Mishnah Gittin 9:10, William Davidson edition, CC BY-NC, via Sefaria).

Jesus' route south likely ran down the east side of the Jordan through Perea, avoiding Samaria, then crossed near Jericho. Perea was ruled by Herod Antipas, who held John at Machaerus according to Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2).

Royal courts used eunuchs as officials, like the Ethiopian treasurer in Acts 8:27. The Torah barred them from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1), but Isaiah 56:3-5 promises them 'a name better than that of sons and daughters.'

DEBATES.h: What does 'except for sexual immorality' allow?
DEBATES.p: Some read porneia as adultery, allowing divorce and remarriage; others as unlawful marriages (Leviticus 18) or betrothal unfaithfulness. Mark and Luke give no exception (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18).
His exception resembles Shammai's view, but He grounds marriage in creation and calls remarriage adultery, going beyond either school.
Most read 19:12 of voluntary celibacy for the kingdom's sake (compare 1 Corinthians 7:7). Origen was said to have taken it literally, which the church rejected.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Mark's account runs to Mark 10:12, not 10:11; verse 12 adds the case of a wife who divorces her husband.
The video attributes 'preferred another woman' to Hillel. The Mishnah credits that view to Rabbi Akiva; Beit Hillel's example is a burned or over-salted dish (Gittin 9:10).
The 'more original the weightier' rule is not given a source in the video. Jesus' appeal to creation is clear in the text either way.
Exodus 21:10-11 concerns a slave-wife (21:7-11); the LSB reads 'another woman.'
The idea that Israel took an ungodly view of divorce 'in Egyptian captivity' is the video's suggestion, not something the text says.

The captions write 'Shamai,' 'Shmai,' 'Shmama' and 'Shemi' for Shammai, 'Hel' and 'Hella' for Hillel, 'Unix' for eunuchs, 'Herodiius' for Herodias, 'Meabbah' and 'Massa' for Meribah and Massah, and 'antiene' for ante-Nicene.

QUESTIONS: Why does Jesus answer a question about Moses by going back to creation?
What do Deuteronomy 24 and Exodus 21 protect, and whom?
How does 'hardness of heart' connect the Pharisees to Israel in the wilderness?
What changes when you see marriage as an agreement with God, not only between two people?
Do you read Scripture to know about God or to know God? What would change?
How can a church honor both married and single people 'for the sake of the kingdom'?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: those who truly seek to know God will properly interpret His commandments, because they understand the heart behind them. Proper motivation guides proper interpretation. The teacher recalls studying theology, church history and doctrine as a young believer without appreciating what broke God's heart or truly pleased Him, until a mentor taught him to read the Bible first of all to know God. The historical context and original languages matter, but they exist to serve that goal. Are you reading the word of God to know God, His heart and His desires? If you do, you will interpret His word correctly, including the institution of marriage.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before your next reading, pray Jeremiah 9:24 and ask, 'What does this passage show me about who God is?' Write one sentence about God, not only about the text.

   (video) Isn't that what the Pharisees are doing now, testing Jesus? The commands at Sinai were meant to reform the practice of divorce over time.
4. Matthew 19:9; 5:32: Except for sexual immorality
   Matthew 19 (Matthew 19:9, LSB): "And I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.”"
   Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:32, LSB): "but I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except for the reason of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery."
   (video) The only permission Jesus allows is porneia, sexual immorality, recalling the Sermon on the Mount. It is a broad term, but it narrowed things considerably for first-century Jews.

## Read Torah to know God
1. Matthew 19:10-12: Better not to marry?
   Eunuchs Matthew 19:12: "For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are also eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to accept this, let him accept it.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+19:12
   (video) The disciples struggle with the stricter view. Jesus says in so many words: if you have a problem with the sacredness and finality of marriage, don't get married. Be a eunuch for the sake of God's kingdom.
   (video) In the first century there were two kinds of eunuchs: those born without reproductive parts, and those castrated to serve as royal or government officials.
2. Matthew 12:7; Hosea 6:6: If you had known what this means
   Jesus (Matthew 12:7, LSB): "But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent."
   Hosea (Hosea 6:6, LSB): "For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, / And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings."
   (video) How could teachers who memorized God's law miss the point of divorce? Jesus already told us when His disciples were challenged over the Sabbath: they would not have condemned them if they understood the heart of God.
3. Jeremiah 9:23-24: That he understands and knows Me
   Remez Jeremiah 9:23-24: "Thus says Yahweh, “Let not a wise man boast in his wisdom, and let not the mighty man boast in his might; let not a rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am Yahweh who shows lovingkindness, justice, and righteousness on earth; for I delight in these things,” declares Yahweh." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Jeremiah+9:23-24
   (video) It has always been God's desire that His people know Him. Someone who camps out in Genesis 1 and 2 to know the God who reveals Himself there would not be surprised by Jesus' answer.
   (video) The Pharisees were entrusted with the oracles of God (Romans 3:2), yet read Torah to know Torah instead of to know God: the same activity with two different motivations. (Romans 3:2)
4. The lesson: Proper motivation guides proper interpretation
   (video) Those who truly seek to know God will properly interpret His commandments, because they understand the heart behind them. Those who seek only to know His commandments will often misinterpret them.
   (video) The teacher describes studying theology early on to know what God's word said, and later learning from a mentor to read it to know God. The result is greater intimacy with the Lord and a deeper love for Him.

## Key people
- The Pharisees: Test Jesus on divorce, likely as a trap. [Background] Mark has Jesus first ask, 'What did Moses command you?' (Mark 10:3).
- Shammai: His school allowed divorce only for unchastity; Jesus' answer is closer to it. The captions write 'Shamai,' 'Shmai' and 'Shemi.' [Background] A leading sage of the late first century BC, Hillel's contemporary.
- Hillel: His school allowed divorce for almost any reason, even a bad meal. The captions write 'Hel' and 'Hella.' [Background] Mishnah Gittin 9:10 records Beit Hillel's view; the 'better looking woman' view is Rabbi Akiva's.
- Herod Antipas and Herodias: Herod married his brother's wife and killed John for speaking against it. [Background] Matthew tells the story in 14:3-12. The captions write 'Herodiius.'
- The disciples: Struggle with the stricter view: better not to marry. [Background] Mark says they asked again in the house (Mark 10:10).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Jesus' Galilean base, which He now leaves (19:1).
- Perea (named in the video): 'The region of Judea beyond the Jordan' (19:1), east of the river, where this exchange happens.
- Jericho: On the road ahead; He leaves Jericho in 20:29.
- Jerusalem (named in the video): Where Jesus is heading to be arrested and crucified.

## Key terms
- Certificate of divorce: The written document a husband gave his wife (Deuteronomy 24:1), freeing her to remarry.
- Some indecency: Hebrew ervat davar in Deuteronomy 24:1, read as sexual immorality or anything out of order.
- Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: The two leading schools of Pharisaic interpretation in Jesus' day.
- One flesh: The union of husband and wife from Genesis 2:24.
- Hardness of heart: Stubborn refusal toward God; an echo of Psalm 95:8.
- Eunuch: A man born without, or deprived of, reproductive ability; often a royal official. The captions write 'Unix.'

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Divorce in the first century: A husband could divorce by giving a certificate; a wife generally could not initiate. The Mishnah records three views on Deuteronomy 24:1: Shammai's (only sexual misconduct), Hillel's (even a burned dish) and Rabbi Akiva's (even finding someone better looking) (Mishnah Gittin 9:10, William Davidson edition, CC BY-NC, via Sefaria).
- Judea beyond the Jordan: Jesus' route south likely ran down the east side of the Jordan through Perea, avoiding Samaria, then crossed near Jericho. Perea was ruled by Herod Antipas, who held John at Machaerus according to Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.2).
- Eunuchs at court: Royal courts used eunuchs as officials, like the Ethiopian treasurer in Acts 8:27. The Torah barred them from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1), but Isaiah 56:3-5 promises them 'a name better than that of sons and daughters.'

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Like then as to sever flesh is a horrible thing, so also to divorce a wife is unlawful." Homilies on Matthew 62, on 19:6. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "from one root they sprung, and into one body came they together" Homilies on Matthew 62, on 19:4-5. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "He would not have studied to show that His own precepts agreed with those of old." Homilies on Matthew 62, on 19:4-8. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- What does 'except for sexual immorality' allow? Some read porneia as adultery, allowing divorce and remarriage; others as unlawful marriages (Leviticus 18) or betrothal unfaithfulness. Mark and Luke give no exception (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18).
- Did Jesus side with Shammai? His exception resembles Shammai's view, but He grounds marriage in creation and calls remarriage adultery, going beyond either school.
- Eunuchs for the kingdom Most read 19:12 of voluntary celibacy for the kingdom's sake (compare 1 Corinthians 7:7). Origen was said to have taken it literally, which the church rejected.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Mark's account runs to Mark 10:12, not 10:11; verse 12 adds the case of a wife who divorces her husband.
- The video attributes 'preferred another woman' to Hillel. The Mishnah credits that view to Rabbi Akiva; Beit Hillel's example is a burned or over-salted dish (Gittin 9:10).
- The 'more original the weightier' rule is not given a source in the video. Jesus' appeal to creation is clear in the text either way.
- Exodus 21:10-11 concerns a slave-wife (21:7-11); the LSB reads 'another woman.'
- The idea that Israel took an ungodly view of divorce 'in Egyptian captivity' is the video's suggestion, not something the text says.
- The captions write 'Shamai,' 'Shmai,' 'Shmama' and 'Shemi' for Shammai, 'Hel' and 'Hella' for Hillel, 'Unix' for eunuchs, 'Herodiius' for Herodias, 'Meabbah' and 'Massa' for Meribah and Massah, and 'antiene' for ante-Nicene.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why does Jesus answer a question about Moses by going back to creation?
2. What do Deuteronomy 24 and Exodus 21 protect, and whom?
3. How does 'hardness of heart' connect the Pharisees to Israel in the wilderness?
4. What changes when you see marriage as an agreement with God, not only between two people?
5. Do you read Scripture to know about God or to know God? What would change?
6. How can a church honor both married and single people 'for the sake of the kingdom'?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: those who truly seek to know God will properly interpret His commandments, because they understand the heart behind them. Proper motivation guides proper interpretation. The teacher recalls studying theology, church history and doctrine as a young believer without appreciating what broke God's heart or truly pleased Him, until a mentor taught him to read the Bible first of all to know God. The historical context and original languages matter, but they exist to serve that goal. Are you reading the word of God to know God, His heart and His desires? If you do, you will interpret His word correctly, including the institution of marriage.
- Study note (added): before your next reading, pray Jeremiah 9:24 and ask, 'What does this passage show me about who God is?' Write one sentence about God, not only about the text.
